The fulfilled reader notes that Jesus spoke to 'you', the disciples. Most of the apostles did suffer and die for His name, just as He said.
Betrayal and hatred
shall betray one another, and shall hate one another

Jesus warns that many will fall away and betray and hate one another. In the fulfilled reading, the pressure of persecution would cause some believers to turn against others. Some would give their names to the authorities to save themselves.

In AD 64 Nero arrested Christians after the fire of Rome. Tacitus says those first arrested gave information, and a 'huge crowd' was then convicted. Many were cruelly killed. Christian tradition, recorded later by Eusebius, says Peter and Paul died in Rome under Nero.
Tacitus says that on the information of those first seized, a huge crowd was convicted. Some were burned as torches at night.
Eusebius records the tradition that Paul was beheaded and Peter crucified in Rome under Nero.
Futurist readers expect a great falling away from the faith at the end of the age, often linked to 2 Thessalonians 2:3.
The fulfilled reader answers that Paul already wrote that all in Asia had turned away from him (2 Timothy 1:15). The falling away Jesus described happened in the apostles' generation.
False prophets deceive many
many false prophets shall rise, and shall deceive many

Jesus warns that many false prophets will arise and lead many astray. In the fulfilled reading, these are the false prophets who promised deliverance to Jerusalem during the war. Their false hopes kept people in the city until it was too late.

During the siege of AD 70, the rebel leaders hired prophets to tell the people to wait for help from God. This stopped people from deserting to the Romans. On the day the Temple burned, a false prophet led a crowd up to the Temple to receive 'signs of deliverance'. They died there.
Josephus says the rebel leaders bribed many false prophets to tell the people to wait for God's help, so they would not desert.
Josephus describes deceivers who led crowds into the wilderness, promising signs of freedom.
Futurist readers see false prophets increasing in the last days, often linked to the false prophet of Revelation 13.
The fulfilled reader replies that John said 'many false prophets have gone out into the world' already (1 John 4:1). Josephus shows how these deceivers led many to their deaths.
Love grows cold
the love of many shall wax cold

Jesus warns that because lawlessness will increase, the love of many will grow cold. The fulfilled reading sees this in the spiritual condition of first-century Judea and of some churches. Jesus had already called His hearers 'a wicked and adulterous generation' (Matthew 12:39).

During the war, rival rebel groups in Jerusalem fought and killed one another. From AD 68 the Zealots murdered leading citizens, including the former high priest Ananus. Josephus says no city ever suffered such things and no generation was ever more wicked.
Josephus says no other city ever suffered such misery, and no generation since the world began was more fruitful in wickedness.
Josephus records the murder of the former high priest Ananus by the Zealots and their Idumean allies.
Futurist readers see growing lawlessness and loss of love as marks of the last days before Christ's return.
The fulfilled reader notes that Paul's 'last days' warning was given to Timothy, who was told to turn away from such people (2 Timothy 3:5). The warning fit their own time.
Endure to the end
he that shall endure unto the end

Jesus promises that the one who endures to the end will be saved. In the fulfilled reading, 'the end' is the end of the age in AD 70. 'Saved' here mainly means being rescued from the coming destruction. Believers who held on to His words and fled at the right time would escape alive.

Eusebius records that the Jerusalem church received a warning before the war and left the city. They settled in Pella, a town east of the Jordan. So the Christians of Jerusalem escaped the siege and the slaughter of AD 70.
Eusebius says the Jerusalem church was told by a revelation to leave the city before the war and to live in Pella of Perea.
sozo (σῴζω)
to save, rescue, make safe

The word often means rescue from physical danger, as in Matthew 8:25 ('Lord, save us'). Here the verb for 'endure' is hypomeno, to remain or hold firm. Together they promise rescue for those who stay faithful.
Futurist readers usually take 'the end' as the end of a believer's life or the end of history. They see 'saved' as final salvation.
The fulfilled reader replies that the context is the end of the age asked about in verse 3. Luke 21:18-19 speaks of physical survival: 'not a hair of your head will perish'.
The gospel to the whole world
preached in all the world for a witness

Jesus says the gospel of the kingdom will be preached in the whole world as a witness to all nations, and then the end will come. In the fulfilled reading, 'world' means the inhabited Roman world. The gospel had to reach it before the end of the Old Covenant age in AD 70.

By the early 60s AD, Paul could say the gospel was bearing fruit 'in all the world' (Colossians 1:6). He said it had been preached 'to every creature under heaven' (Colossians 1:23). Churches existed in Judea, Syria, Asia Minor, Greece, Rome and Egypt. The Temple fell a few years later, in AD 70.
Paul says the gospel has been proclaimed to every creature under heaven.
Paul says the faith of the Roman believers is spoken of throughout the whole world.
oikoumene (οἰκουμένη)
the inhabited world

This word is used in Luke 2:1, where Augustus orders 'all the world' to be registered. That meant the Roman Empire. It is also used in Acts 11:28 for a famine 'over all the world' under Claudius. The fulfilled reading takes it the same way here.
Futurist readers see this as the task of world mission, still to be completed among every people group before Christ returns.
The fulfilled reader agrees that mission continues today. But this verse uses Paul's own word for the known world. Paul said the task had already been done in his day.
The abomination of desolation
the abomination of desolation, spoken of by Daniel

Jesus gives the disciples a clear sign: when they see the 'abomination of desolation' that Daniel spoke of standing in the holy place, they must act. Luke's parallel explains it: 'when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies' (Luke 21:20). Fulfilled interpreters differ on details. Some point to the Roman armies, some to Zealot desecration of the Temple, and some to both.

In AD 66 the Roman general Cestius Gallus surrounded Jerusalem and then withdrew. In AD 67-68 the Zealots occupied the Temple and appointed a high priest by lot. In AD 70, after the Temple burned, Roman soldiers set up their standards in the Temple court and offered sacrifices to them.
Josephus describes Cestius Gallus attacking Jerusalem in AD 66 and then suddenly withdrawing.
Josephus says the Zealots took over the Temple and chose an unfit man as high priest by lot.
Josephus says the Romans brought their standards into the Temple court and offered sacrifices to them.
bdelygma (βδέλυγμα)
abomination, something detestable
In the Greek Old Testament this word often describes idols and idolatry. The phrase 'abomination of desolation' means a detestable thing that brings ruin. It comes from Daniel 9:27, 11:31 and 12:11.
Futurist readers expect a future Antichrist to set up an idol or image in a rebuilt Temple, in the middle of a seven-year tribulation.
The fulfilled reader replies that Jesus said 'when you see', speaking to His disciples. Luke 21:20 explains the sign in terms of armies around Jerusalem, which they did see.
Flee to the mountains
let them which be in Judaea flee into the mountains

Jesus tells those in Judea to flee to the mountains when they see the sign. In the fulfilled reading, this local detail shows the passage is about first-century Judea, not the whole world. The safe place was outside the doomed city.

After Cestius Gallus withdrew from Jerusalem in late AD 66, many people left the city. Eusebius says the Christians went to Pella, east of the Jordan. When the siege came in AD 70, the believers were already gone.
Eusebius says the believers left Jerusalem before the war and lived in Pella, a city of Perea.
Josephus says that after Cestius' defeat many leading Jews left the city 'as from a sinking ship'.
Futurist readers apply this to Jewish people in Israel at a future time. Some see the flight as a refuge in places like Petra.
The fulfilled reader replies that the history matches closely. The sign came, there was a short break, and the believers fled before the city was shut in.
Do not go back into the house
Let him which is on the housetop not come down

Jesus says the person on the roof must not go down to fetch belongings. Houses in Judea had flat roofs used for work, rest and prayer. The fulfilled reading sees this as practical advice for first-century people: when the sign comes, leave at once.

In a Judean town, a person on a flat roof could see an approaching army. Outside stairs often led from the roof to the street. So a person could flee without going through the house. The danger grew quickly once Roman forces moved through Judea from AD 67 onward.
Futurist readers take this as a picture of the speed needed in a future crisis. Some apply it to Israel at the end of the age.
The fulfilled reader notes that the details fit first-century Judea: flat roofs, outside stairs and towns near an advancing army.
Do not go back for your cloak
Neither let him which is in the field return back

Jesus says the worker in the field must not return home for a cloak. A worker usually left the outer cloak at home or at the edge of the field. The fulfilled reading sees an urgent call to flee without delay, as Lot's family was told not to look back.

Fields lay on open, lower ground, where workers would be easy to see. During Vespasian's campaigns of AD 67-68, Roman troops moved through the countryside of Galilee, Perea and Judea. Many people who delayed were killed or captured.
Josephus describes Roman forces in Perea in AD 68 killing and capturing many people who had fled from Gadara.
Futurist readers see this as a warning for a future time of sudden danger, especially for Israel.
The fulfilled reader replies that the setting is a farming land under threat of invasion. It matches Judea in the years AD 66-70.
Woe to mothers
woe unto them that are with child

Jesus grieves for pregnant women and nursing mothers, who would find it hard to flee. The fulfilled reading links this with His words to the 'daughters of Jerusalem' on the way to the cross (Luke 23:28-29). Those days would bring great suffering to families.

During the siege of AD 70 the famine in Jerusalem became terrible. Josephus tells of a woman named Mary, daughter of Eleazar, who killed and ate her own child. This recalls the curses of Deuteronomy 28:53-57.
Josephus tells of a woman in the siege who, starving and in despair, killed and ate her infant son.
Josephus describes how the famine destroyed whole families and how children snatched food from parents.
Futurist readers apply this to mothers during a future great tribulation.
The fulfilled reader replies that the warning was fulfilled in the siege of Jerusalem. Applying it to mothers today can cause needless fear.
Not in winter or on the Sabbath
pray ye that your flight be not in the winter

Jesus tells the disciples to pray that their flight will not be in winter or on a Sabbath. Winter rain made roads hard and rivers high. On the Sabbath, city gates might be closed and travel was limited by custom. These details fit a Jewish setting in first-century Judea.

In early AD 68, people fleeing from Gadara were trapped by the Jordan River, which was swollen by rain. Many drowned or were killed. Under the law, travel on the Sabbath was limited. Nehemiah had once shut Jerusalem's gates on the Sabbath.
Josephus says the Jordan was swollen with rain and the fleeing crowd could not cross. Many were killed or drowned.
phyge (φυγή)
flight, escape
The word means running away from danger. Jesus speaks of a real escape on foot from a real place. The concern about the Sabbath points to people living under Jewish custom in Judea.
Futurist readers say the Sabbath detail shows that Jewish believers in a future Israel are in view.
The fulfilled reader replies that the Sabbath detail fits the first-century disciples, who lived among Sabbath-keeping people in Judea. It does not need a distant future setting.
then shall be great tribulation

Jesus says there will be great distress, such as has not been since the beginning of the world, nor ever will be. The fulfilled reading sees this as the siege and fall of Jerusalem in AD 70. It was a unique judgment on the city and its Temple at the end of the Old Covenant age. Luke calls it 'wrath on this people' (Luke 21:23).

Titus besieged Jerusalem from about April to September AD 70. Famine, civil war inside the city and Roman attacks killed vast numbers. The Temple burned in late August. Josephus gives 1,100,000 dead and 97,000 taken captive in the whole war.
Josephus says 97,000 were taken captive during the whole war and 1,100,000 died during the siege.
In his preface Josephus says the misfortunes of all people since the world began fall short of those of the Jews.
kosmos (κόσμος)
world, ordered world

Here Jesus says 'since the beginning of the world (kosmos)'. This is a different word from oikoumene in verse 14. The phrase 'such as has not been … nor ever will be' is a familiar prophetic way to stress how severe a judgment is (compare Ezekiel 5:9).
Futurist readers place the great tribulation in the future, as a worldwide time of trouble. Some also point out that later events, such as the Holocaust, killed more people.
The fulfilled reader replies that Jesus' words describe a covenant judgment on Jerusalem, not a contest of numbers. 'Nor ever will be' shows it was a one-time event.
The days shortened
except those days should be shortened

Jesus says that if those days were not shortened, no one would survive. But for the sake of the elect, they will be cut short. In the fulfilled reading, 'no flesh' means no one in the land. 'The elect' are the believers, whom God protected.

The war lasted from AD 66 to 70, about three and a half years. Cestius' sudden withdrawal in AD 66 gave believers time to flee. Titus' siege itself lasted only about five months. His quick wall around the city ended the siege faster than many expected.
Eusebius says the Jerusalem church escaped to Pella before the war.
Josephus says the Romans built a wall around the whole city in three days.
Josephus says Titus admitted that God had helped him take the city.
Futurist readers see this as God limiting a future seven-year tribulation, so that some will survive until Christ returns.
The fulfilled reader notes that the war on Judea lasted about three and a half years. Some in this reading link this to the 'forty-two months' of Revelation 13:5.
Do not believe 'Here is the Christ'
Lo, here is Christ, or there; believe it not

Jesus warns that during the crisis people will say, 'Look, here is the Christ!' The disciples must not believe them. The fulfilled reading sees this as a warning aimed at the time of the war and siege. At that time leaders rose up claiming to bring deliverance.

In AD 66 Menahem, a descendant of Judas the Galilean, entered the Temple dressed as a king, and was then killed. Later, Simon bar Giora led rebels in the city. When captured in AD 70, he appeared in white and purple robes. He was executed in Rome during Titus' triumph.
Josephus says Menahem went up to the Temple in royal clothing with armed followers, and was later killed.
Josephus says Simon bar Giora rose out of the ground at the Temple site dressed in white and purple.
Futurist readers see this as a warning against claims of Christ's return in the last days before His real coming.
The fulfilled reader replies that the setting is the time of the tribulation in Judea. In that time, men did claim royal and saving roles.
Great signs and wonders
shall shew great signs and wonders

Jesus warns that false christs and false prophets will perform great signs to deceive, if possible, even the elect. The fulfilled reading points to the magicians and false prophets of Acts and to the prophets of the siege. They promised miracles of deliverance.

Acts records Simon the sorcerer in Samaria and Bar-Jesus, also called Elymas, in Cyprus. During the siege of AD 70, prophets told the people to wait for signs from God. On the day the Temple burned, a crowd followed one such promise to their deaths.
Josephus says many prophets were bribed to tell the people to wait for God's help. He says deceivers easily persuade people in distress.
Simon of Samaria amazed people with magic and claimed to be someone great.
Futurist readers expect a future false prophet who will do great signs, as in Revelation 13:13-14.
The fulfilled reader replies that the disciples needed this warning in their own day. The deceivers Josephus describes fit Jesus' words.
Told beforehand
Behold, I have told you before

Jesus reminds the disciples that He has told them these things in advance. In the fulfilled reading, He speaks to men who would live through the events. He prepared them so they would not be caught by fear or deception. God reveals His plans to His servants before He acts.

The Jerusalem believers remembered His warning about forty years later. They fled before the siege, as Eusebius records. The prophecy given in about AD 30-33 guided their actions in the crisis of AD 66-70.
Eusebius says the church left Jerusalem because of a revelation given before the war.
Futurist readers see this as a word for believers in every age, especially those living at the end of history.
The fulfilled reader agrees that all believers can learn from it. But 'I have told you' was spoken to the four disciples, who would see the events.
Not in the desert or the inner rooms
Behold, he is in the desert; go not forth

Jesus warns: if people say the Messiah is in the wilderness, do not go out. If they say He is in the inner rooms, do not believe it. The fulfilled reading sees two kinds of false hope: leaders who led crowds into the desert, and prophets who promised rescue inside the Temple.

Under Felix, deceivers led crowds into the wilderness, and the Egyptian prophet's followers were scattered. On the day the Temple burned in AD 70, about 6,000 people gathered in a Temple portico. A false prophet had promised signs there, and they all died in the fire. After the war, Jonathan the weaver led people into the desert in Cyrene.
Josephus says about 6,000 people died in a burning portico of the Temple, because a false prophet had led them there.
Josephus describes deceivers and the Egyptian prophet leading crowds into the wilderness under Felix.
Josephus says Jonathan, a weaver, led poor people into the desert of Cyrene after the war.
Futurist readers apply this to false claims of a secret return of Christ before His visible coming.
The fulfilled reader replies that Josephus records exactly these two kinds of deceivers in the years before and during the war.
Like lightning from east to west
as the lightning cometh out of the east

Jesus says His coming will be like lightning that shines from east to west: sudden, clear and impossible to miss. In the fulfilled reading, His coming here is His coming in judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70. It was not hidden in a desert or a room, but seen by all. The Old Testament often pictures God 'coming' in storm and cloud to judge a nation.

In AD 70 Rome's armies destroyed Jerusalem and the Temple. Fulfilled interpreters see this as the visible sign of Christ's judgment, as He told the high priest (Matthew 26:64). Some in this reading add that the Tenth Legion came up from Jericho in the east and camped on the Mount of Olives.
Josephus says the Tenth Legion came by way of Jericho and camped on the Mount of Olives, east of the city.
parousia (παρουσία)
presence, arrival, coming

In Matthew this word appears only in chapter 24 (verses 3, 27, 37 and 39). It was used for the arrival of a king or official. The fulfilled reading takes it as Christ's presence in judgment on that generation.
Futurist readers take this as Christ's visible, bodily return to earth at the end of history, seen by the whole world.
The fulfilled reader replies that 'coming on the clouds' is prophetic language for God's judgment (Isaiah 19:1). Jesus told Caiaphas that he would see it.
The carcass and the eagles
wheresoever the carcase is, there will the eagles

Jesus says that wherever the carcass is, there the eagles (or vultures) will gather. In the fulfilled reading, the carcass is Jerusalem with its dead Temple system. The eagles are the Roman legions, whose standard was the eagle (aquila). The saying also pictures birds gathering over unburied dead.

In AD 70 the Roman army gathered around Jerusalem and took it. Dead bodies filled the streets and were left unburied. After the Temple burned, the soldiers carried their eagle standards into the Temple court and offered sacrifices to them there.
Josephus says the Romans brought their standards into the Temple court, set them up there and offered sacrifices to them.
Josephus says the lanes of the city were blocked with dead bodies.
aetos (ἀετός)
eagle, or vulture

The word can mean an eagle or a vulture, since both gather at dead bodies. Deuteronomy 28:49 warns that a nation will come 'as swift as the eagle' to judge Israel. The Roman legions marched under the eagle standard.
Futurist readers take this as a picture of judgment at Christ's return. Some link it to the birds gathering after the battle in Revelation 19:17-18.
The fulfilled reader replies that the eagle was Rome's own emblem. The covenant curse of Deuteronomy 28:49 fits the Roman armies around Jerusalem.
Sun, moon and stars go dark
shall the sun be darkened, and the moon

The fulfilled reading takes this as the prophets' language for the fall of a ruling power, not the end of the physical universe. Isaiah used darkened sun and falling stars for the fall of Babylon, and Ezekiel used them for Egypt. In Genesis the lights 'rule' the day and night, and in Joseph's dream they stand for a family's rulers. So Jesus is saying that the rulers of the old covenant order in Jerusalem would be put out, right after the tribulation of those days.
The collapse of Jerusalem's leadership and Temple order when the city fell to Titus in AD 70, immediately after the siege.
Babylon's fall is described as stars, sun and moon giving no light. Babylon fell to the Medes and Persians, yet the sky did not literally go dark.
God says He will cover the heavens and darken the stars when He puts out Pharaoh, a judgment on Egypt by the king of Babylon.
Futurist readers expect literal signs in the sky at Christ's bodily return at the end of history. Others see both a first-century and a final fulfilment.
The same words were used of nations that fell long ago, and no one expects those skies to have gone black. 'Immediately after' ties the signs to the tribulation Jesus had just described.
they shall see the Son of man coming

In the Old Testament, the Lord 'rides on a cloud' when He comes to judge a nation, as in Isaiah 19:1 against Egypt. In this reading, Jesus claims that same role from Daniel 7:13. The 'tribes of the earth' are taken as the tribes of the land of Israel, who mourn (Zechariah 12:10-12). The 'sign' is the judgment itself: the people would see, in the city's fall, that the Son of Man now reigned.
The judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70, which this reading identifies with the coming (Parousia) of the Son of Man in power.
Jesus told the high priest and council that they would see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven.
Josephus reports that before sunset, chariots and armed troops were seen running among the clouds and surrounding the cities (spring AD 66).
Tacitus also records armies seen clashing in the sky and the Temple lit by fire from the clouds.
earth, land
The Greek word can mean the whole earth or a particular land. This reading takes 'all the tribes of the ge' as the tribes of Israel's land, as in Zechariah 12:12, where families of the land mourn.
Futurist and most historic readers see Christ's visible, bodily return, seen by the whole world. Some partial preterists read verse 30 as AD 70 but keep a future bodily return taught in other texts.
Cloud-coming is God's judgment language in the prophets. Jesus told His own judges that they would see it, so the event fell within their lifetime.
The trumpet and the gathering
he shall send his angels with a great sound

The Greek angelos means 'messenger', and it is used of human messengers such as John the Baptist (Matthew 11:10). In this reading, the 'angels' are gospel messengers. The great trumpet echoes Isaiah 27:13, where a trumpet calls scattered exiles to worship. Once the old order fell, the elect would be gathered from every direction into the one people of God, the opposite of Jeremiah's scattering of Elam to the four winds.
The gathering of believers from every nation into the church, carried on with new freedom after the Temple system ended in AD 70.
A great trumpet sounds, and those lost in Assyria and Egypt come to worship the Lord at Jerusalem.
Moses promised that God would gather His people even from the farthest part of heaven.
Futurist readers see a literal angelic gathering of the elect at Christ's return, either the rapture or the regathering of Israel. Many other readers link it to the final resurrection.

The words 'from one end of heaven to the other' come from Deuteronomy 30:4 and describe a gathering of people, not a trip into the sky. The verse sits within the 'this generation' timeframe of verse 34.
The lesson of the fig tree
Now learn a parable of the fig tree

Jesus gives a plain lesson from nature. When a fig tree puts out soft leaves, summer is near. In the same way, when the disciples saw the signs He had listed, they would know the end was near. This reading also notes the season. Leaves come in spring, and the siege of Jerusalem began in spring, at Passover. Luke adds 'and all the trees', so the point is the season, not a symbol for a nation.
Titus surrounded Jerusalem in the spring of AD 70, a few days before Passover, when crowds of pilgrims filled the city.
Three legions camped near the city, and the tenth legion camped on the Mount of Olives, where Jesus had spoken.
Josephus says most of the dead had come for the Feast of Unleavened Bread and were shut in by the siege.
Many dispensational writers took the fig tree as the modern State of Israel (1948), with the end coming within a generation after that. Others see only a general lesson about reading the signs.
Luke's 'all the trees' shows it is an ordinary picture of the seasons. The lesson was given to the disciples, about signs they themselves would see.
Near, even at the doors
know that it is near, even at the doors

'You' means the disciples sitting with Jesus on the Mount of Olives; Mark 13:3 names Peter, James, John and Andrew. When they saw 'all these things', they would know the end was at the door. James, writing to first-century believers, uses the same picture: the Judge is standing at the door. In this reading, the early church heard this as a nearness they would live to see.
The signs of the AD 60s, and above all armies around Jerusalem (Luke 21:20). Cestius Gallus surrounded the city in AD 66 and then withdrew.
James tells his readers that the Judge is standing at the door.
Eusebius says the Jerusalem church was warned by a revelation to leave the city before the war, and settled in Pella.
Futurist readers say 'you' means the generation that will see the signs at the end of the age, whoever that may be.
Jesus answered the disciples' own question (Matthew 24:3), so 'you' most naturally means them. The early church acted on the warning and fled.
This generation will not pass
This generation shall not pass

This is the key time text of the discourse. In Matthew, 'this generation' always means the people living when Jesus spoke (Matthew 11:16; Matthew 23:36). Just a day earlier, Jesus said that all the blood of the prophets would come upon 'this generation'. Jesus said 'this', not 'that'. In Scripture a generation is often about forty years, and the city fell about forty years after He spoke.
Jerusalem and the Temple fell in AD 70, about forty years after Jesus spoke (about AD 30-33).
Jesus says all these things will come upon this generation, speaking to the leaders in front of Him.
Israel wandered forty years until the whole generation that had done evil was gone.
The Temple burned on the tenth of Av, about late August AD 70.
generation; the people alive at one time

Standard Greek lexicons give the main sense as people born and living at about the same time, 'contemporaries'. A different word, genos, means race or kind. Some futurist notes read genea as 'race' (the Jewish people); preterists answer that the word does not mean that in Matthew.
Futurist readers take it as the generation alive when the end-time signs begin, or as the Jewish race surviving until the end. C. S. Lewis called it 'the most embarrassing verse in the Bible'.
In this reading there is nothing embarrassing in it. Jesus said His hearers would see it, and they did. Every other use of 'this generation' in Matthew means His contemporaries.
Heaven and earth will pass away
Heaven and earth shall pass away

This reading does not take 'heaven and earth' here as the physical universe. It takes it as the covenant world centred on the Temple. Isaiah 51:16 links God's 'planting the heavens' with making Israel His people. Josephus says the parts of the Tabernacle pictured the earth and sea, and heaven. Jesus had said the law would stand 'till heaven and earth pass' (Matthew 5:18). When the Temple fell, the old covenant order passed away, and the Word of Christ remained.
The destruction of the Temple in AD 70 ended the old covenant system of priesthood and sacrifice (Hebrews 8:13).
Josephus says the outer parts of the Tabernacle stood for land and sea, open to people, while the inner room stood for heaven, kept for God.
